title: Patron of ecology (1979)
hook: John Paul II names Francis patron of those who care for creation

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Capuchins, a hooded reform that went back to Francis's poverty. Your line was the hooded friars.

Brother Sun. Sister Moon and the stars. Brother Wind. Sister Water. Brother Fire. It sounds like a roll call at a family reunion, and in a way it is. These are the names Francis gives the world in a song in his own Italian dialect, the Canticle of the Creatures. Tradition says he made it near the end of his life, sick, his eyes so bad he could barely stand the light. A man who could hardly see the sun called it his brother. Centuries later, a pope looked at that song and gave Francis a new job. Today's word is the job.
screen: `BROTHER SUN. SISTER MOON.` → `A SONG FROM A SICK MAN.` → `A NEW JOB FOR FRANCIS.`

segments.voice: Pope John Paul II named Francis the patron of those who care for creation, the patron of ecology. A patron, for Catholics, is a saint in heaven asked to pray for a particular people or work. So anyone who plants a tree has, in Catholic eyes, a friend in brown. Why Francis? Because of the Canticle. It praises God for the sun, beautiful and radiant, who brings the day. For wind and air and every kind of weather. For water, useful and humble and precious and pure. For fire, bright and strong, who lights the night. Then comes the surprise. Francis doesn't call the earth brother. He calls her our sister and our mother, who feeds us and brings forth fruit and colored flowers and grass. Our line borrows the family word; the point is kinship. For Francis, creation isn't scenery. It's family, all of it singing back to its maker. The Bible gives the job from the start. In Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims, God puts the man in the garden "to dress it, and to keep it." To tend it and guard it, not to own it. And the book of Daniel has a song inviting every creature in: "All ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord." So a patron of ecology isn't a saint of recycling bins. He's a saint who heard the world praying, and took his place in the choir.
screen: `A PATRON PRAYS FOR A PEOPLE OR A WORK.` · `SUN, WIND, WATER, FIRE: ALL PRAISE.` · `EARTH: OUR SISTER AND OUR MOTHER.` · `TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.` · then, large: `ALL YE WORKS OF THE LORD, BLESS THE LORD.`

segments.voice: If you can step outside, walk a few steps, pick up three pieces of litter, a wrapper, a bottle cap, and carry them to a bin; if you can't go out, clear one small mess in the room you're in. As you do, notice you're handling a small corner of the earth Francis called sister and mother, and if you pray, thank God for one creature you can see right now.
Patron of ecology. Francis, named by a pope as the saint who prays for those who care for creation, because he sang about the sun and the earth as family. Today's word.
Your line: brother earth. Sun, water and earth, all one family. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Francis in early October, and some parishes bless animals on or near that day; Catholic groups who work for the care of creation often take Francis as their patron.

notes: The index carry is 'brother earth', but the Canticle calls the earth 'sora nostra matre terra' (our sister, Mother Earth). The script keeps the carry exactly and says openly that the line borrows the family word, not Francis's exact one. A Keeper may wish to change the outline carry to 'sister earth' (separate, owner-approved edit).
Claims rule: the title's date (1979, the bull Inter Sanctos) is not repeated in the voice. Confirm the paraphrase 'patron of those who care for creation / patron of ecology'.

Canticle paraphrased (no pre-1929 translation on the public-domain list). Confirm the adjectives: sun beautiful and radiant; water useful, humble, precious and chaste ('pure' used); fire bright/beautiful, robust and strong, lighting the night; earth who sustains and governs us and brings forth fruit with colored flowers and herbs.
'Tradition says he made it near the end of his life, sick and nearly blind' follows Franciscan sources (composed at San Damiano c. 1225). Confirm.
Trapdoor: the ambiguity of 'per' (for/by/through) in the Canticle is a common point in Franciscan scholarship; confirm the wording.
